meta.tagline: A capital between fjord and forest, with an opera roof you can walk on

pills: You can climb the opera roof

overview.title: Welcome to Oslo
overview.intro: Oslo is a capital wedged between two natures: an island-dotted fjord in front, an endless forest behind. The city uses both not as decoration but as daily life — the man leaving his morning meeting is in a fjord sauna by noon, and the metro's last stop connects to a ski trail. You walk on the opera house's roof, stand before Munch's Scream, peel fresh shrimp on the quay. Oslo doesn't show off; but it is one of the calmest answers to the question 'what does living well look like'.

local_word.definition: 'Open-air life': the daily, almost religious bond Norwegians keep with nature. Rain is no excuse — 'there's no bad weather, only bad clothing' is this philosophy's founding proverb.

rules.title: Nature is part of the city — use it
rules.description: The city ferry reaches the fjord islands on a normal ticket, and the forest metro (line 1) drops you at a trailhead in half an hour. Whoever thinks Oslo is just its centre has missed half the city.

rules.title: Prepare your wallet for Norway
rules.description: Oslo is expensive and doesn't hide it: restaurants and alcohol melt a budget fast. The balance is the local way: canteen or bakery at noon, one good restaurant at night, happy hour for the beer.

rules.title: Cash is forgotten — the card does the talking
rules.description: Norway is nearly cashless: card and phone work everywhere, coins nowhere. Transport tickets are bought in the app — looking for a paper ticket is a waste of time.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: Flytoget express 19 min · regular train half price

quick_facts.label: Language
quick_facts.sub: English fluent as a mother tongue

tip.label: The Oslo philosophy
tip.text: An Oslo local never spends a beautiful day indoors: if the sun is out, plans change and everyone is outside. Do the same — save the museums for a rainy day, spend the sunshine on the fjord and the forest.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Ruter's single ticket system gathers metro, tram, bus and the fjord ferries under one roof: one ticket, the whole city — islands included.

items.title: Airport to the centre
items.description: The Flytoget express reaches Central Station in 19 minutes; the regular regional train (Vy) does the same trip minutes slower at half the price. In this city a taxi is the last resort.

items.title: The metro (T-bane) — a network that opens into forest
items.description: Five lines merge in the centre and scatter into nature at the ends: line 1 drops you at the forest paths of Frognerseteren, the Sognsvann line at a lakeside. Centre to wilderness: 30 minutes.

items.title: The tram classics
items.description: Tram 12 is like the city's sightseeing line: it ties together Vigeland Park, Aker Brygge and Gamlebyen. The blue trams are the constant figures of Oslo street photography.

items.title: The fjord ferries
items.description: Ferries from Aker Brygge reach Hovedøya, Gressholmen and the other islands on a normal Ruter ticket: in summer the island beaches, monastery ruins and picnic lawns are the city's swimming pool.

items.title: The centre and shore on foot
items.description: The harbour promenade (Havnepromenaden) walks end to end from the Opera past Akershus Fortress to Aker Brygge: a 9 km route marked by orange towers, the city's best free tour.

callout.label: Ferry tip
callout.text: On a summer evening take the Hovedøya ferry and return on the last departure: from the island side the city skyline, the opera and the Barcode towers reflect on the water at sunset — for the price of a city ticket, not a tour boat.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: Oslo's districts don't hide their characters: the centre practical, Grünerløkka bohemian, Frogner elegant, Sørenga brand-new and right on the water.

local_word.definition: The name of the forest belt wrapped around Oslo: by law the city cannot grow beyond its border. An Oslo local's weekend plan is often one word: 'we're going to Marka' — skiing, hiking or simply silence.

items.name: Sentrum (around Karl Johan)
items.description: Between the station, the palace, the opera and the main street: walk everywhere, reach every line. High hotel density, less character — the efficient base for a short visit.

items.name: Grünerløkka
items.description: The old workers' quarter's new life of coffee roasters, bars and vintage shops: walks along the Akerselva river, second-hand markets on Sundays. Oslo's young heart beats here.

items.name: Frogner and Majorstuen
items.description: The neighbourhood of embassies, art nouveau apartment houses and Vigeland Park: calm streets, smart cafés, park runs. The showcase of classic Oslo life.

items.name: Aker Brygge and Tjuvholmen
items.description: Modern life on the wharf: fjord-view hotels, the Astrup Fearnley museum, waterfront restaurants. Prices high, sunset included.

items.name: Sørenga and Bjørvika
items.description: The new waterside quarter behind the opera: a swimming pier (Sørenga Sjøbad), the Munch museum and the Barcode towers. A modern base for sea-bathers and architecture lovers.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Oslo changes shape with the seasons: a fjord city in summer, a ski city in winter, and two short, lovely transitions in between.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Awakening and 17 May
items.subtitle: Spring · Terraces, national day joy
items.description: The snow retreats, the terraces open, and the city gorges on light. On Constitution Day, 17 May, all of Norway takes to the streets in national dress (bunad): parades, ice cream and brass bands — the year's most colourful day.

callout.label: 17 May tip
callout.text: If you're in Oslo on 17 May, get to Karl Johan early: the children's parade passes the palace and the royal family waves from the balcony. Don't skip your hotel breakfast that day — finding a table in town is hard.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Fjord Season
items.subtitle: Summer · Island beaches, light until 11 pm
items.description: The days are long, the fjord counts as warm, the islands fill with picnickers: the city moves outdoors. Utepils (outdoor beer) season peaks; hotels are relatively calm because the Norwegians are on holiday too.

callout.label: July tip
callout.text: Give one evening to a fjord sauna: warm up in the floating saunas opposite the Opera, jump into the fjord, warm up again. Book a few days ahead — Oslo's new classic is overflowing.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Golden Marka
items.subtitle: Autumn · Yellow forests, museum season
items.description: The Marka forest turns gold, the air sharpens, the museums calm down. September is for hiking, October and November for museums and coffee; the first snow sometimes reaches the city in November.

callout.label: September tip
callout.text: At the peak of autumn colour take metro line 1 up to Frognerseteren: apple cake at the restaurant overlooking the fjord through yellow forest, the Holmenkollen ski tower on the way down — Oslo's best half-day view tour.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Ski Capital
items.subtitle: Winter · Skiing by metro, short days, warm drinks
items.description: When the snow falls Oslo returns to its second identity: you ride the metro to the ski trails, skate on frozen lakes, and the cafés switch to candlelight. The days are short, but the city manages the dark well.

callout.label: February tip
callout.text: Even if you can't ski, sled from Frognerseteren down to Midtstuen (the Korketrekkeren run): up by metro ticket, sled rented, 2 km of screaming. The cheapest fun of an Oslo winter.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: The New Nordic wave is strong in Oslo too, but the city's essence is simple: good salmon, shrimp on the quay, a cinnamon bun from the bakery and world-league coffee.

local_word.definition: 'A beer drunk outdoors': the special name a long-wintered people gives to the year's first beer on a sunny terrace. If you see crowded terraces in April sunshine, know that utepils season has officially opened.

items.name: Fresh shrimp on the quay
items.description: Boiled shrimp bought from the boat, peeled on the quay with baguette, mayonnaise and lemon: the best-loved ritual of an Oslo summer. Find a bench on the Aker Brygge pier and defend the shells from the gulls.
items.tag: Summer classic · at the pier's edge

items.name: Salmon and skrei — fjord cooking
items.description: Norwegian salmon is good everywhere, but fish soup and, in season, skrei (the migrating cod) are the city's real pride. The fish halls and the Mathallen counters show the day's fresh catch.

items.name: Brunost — the caramel cheese
items.description: The brown goat's cheese is Norway's odd and lovable classic: caramel-like, on a waffle or the breakfast bread. Be surprised at the first bite, be addicted by the third.

items.name: Kanelbolle and kardemummebolle
items.description: Cinnamon and cardamom buns are the daily contest of Oslo's bakeries: at a good one they don't last past noon. In a city of coffee world champions, bun + filter coffee counts as a meal.
items.tag: From a morning bakery · with coffee

items.name: Pølse med lompe
items.description: A sausage wrapped in potato flatbread (lompe), crowned with mustard and crispy onions: Norway's standing national snack. From petrol station to stadium, the same sincerity everywhere.
items.tag: On your feet · wrapped in lompe

items.name: Craft beer and happy hour arithmetic
items.description: Oslo's micro-brewery scene is strong and its prices brave: the early-hour discounts of Grünerløkka's bars are a budget's friend. Vinmonopolet (the state monopoly) closes at 6 pm, Saturdays at 4 — plan ahead.
items.tag: In Grünerløkka · at the early hour

callout.label: Budget tip
callout.text: The way to manage Oslo's restaurant bill is at lunch: 'dagens rett' (dish of the day) menus run at half the evening price. Ask for water — tap water is free and as clean as the fjord.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone walks the opera roof; these six are Oslo one layer deeper.

items.rarity: An island monastery inside the city
items.name: Hovedøya
items.description: The island ten minutes away by ferry: an 800-year-old monastery ruin, small beaches and pine-shaded picnic lawns. Reached on a normal city ticket — Oslo's cheapest 'holiday'.

items.name: The Akerselva walk
items.description: The river that splits the city descends 8 km between waterfalls and old factories: art schools, coffee roasters and falls under bridges — Oslo's industrial memory. Walk it downhill and break in Grünerløkka.

items.rarity: A sculpture forest above the fjord
items.name: Ekebergparken
items.description: The sculpture park on the ridge where Munch drew the Scream's landscape: an open-air collection from Dalí to Vigeland, in among the trees. Go up by tram — the city and the fjord lie at your feet.

items.name: Damstredet and Telthusbakken
items.description: Eighteenth-century wooden houses two steps from the centre: crooked lanes, coloured façades, garden roses. A five-minute detour, two hundred years of quiet.

items.name: The fjord saunas — Oslo's floating bathhouses
items.description: Warm up in the floating sauna rafts opposite the Opera, then jump into the fjord: ice in winter, cool relief in summer — open all year. The best tradition Oslo has invented in the last decade.

items.name: The Holmenkollen jump tower
items.description: From the top of the legendary ski jump the Oslo fjord turns into a map; the ski museum inside tells a 4,000-year story. Reached by metro — and the tower offers a zipline to the brave.

callout.label: Museum tip
callout.text: At the Munch museum the Scream is not one painting: to protect them, the museum rotates its three versions — which one hangs depends on the hour. Ask at the entrance and plan your floors accordingly.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Oslo is honest; its traps hide in the price tag and in bad planning.

items.name: The airport taxi
items.description: A Gardermoen-to-centre taxi reaches shocking figures; add time on top if there's traffic.
items.instead: Flytoget takes 19 minutes; the regular Vy train does it in 25 at half the price. Even with lots of luggage the train wins — the station is inside the terminal.

items.name: Every meal at Aker Brygge
items.description: The wharf restaurants are masters of adding the view tax: an ordinary dinner leaves a crater in the budget.
items.instead: Have only an utepils on the wharf; eat in Grünerløkka, on Torggata or at Mathallen. The shrimp ritual is on the pier anyway — beautiful without a restaurant.

items.name: Buying the Oslo Pass without doing the maths
items.description: The Oslo Pass only pays off for someone doing 2-3 museums a day; on a walking-and-nature programme the card goes to waste.
items.instead: Write your museum list first, add up the entry fees, then decide. The fjord ferry and public transport are already covered by the cheap Ruter ticket.

items.name: Leaving the alcohol plan for the evening
items.description: Supermarket beer sales end at 8 pm (Saturdays 6 pm), wine and spirits are only at Vinmonopolet, which closes early; at night the shop shelf is literally locked.
items.instead: Plan your drinks in daylight, or use the bars' happy hours. Norwegians arrive at parties with their own bottle — this system is the reason.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Oslo the most expensive things are indoors and the most beautiful things are outdoors: fjord, forest, harbour promenade, opera roof — all free. Save the budget for one good dinner and one sauna; nature pays for the rest.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: An Oslo day from rooftop to fjord

steps.title: Morning on the opera roof
steps.description: Walk the marble slope to the roof: the fjord, the islands and the waking city beneath you. Morning light is at its best on the white marble.

steps.title: Munch or the National Museum
steps.description: Face the Scream: the Munch museum neighbours the opera, the National Museum sits by the harbour. Choose one — both don't fit in a morning.

steps.title: Harbour promenade + shrimp
steps.description: Walk the Havnepromenaden past Akershus Fortress to Aker Brygge; a fresh shrimp + baguette break on the pier.

steps.title: Vigeland Park
steps.description: Tram 12 to Frogner: the human condition in more than 200 sculptures — the photo with the Angry Boy is the classic. The park is free and always open.

steps.title: A Grünerløkka pause
steps.description: Descend along the Akerselva into the neighbourhood: third-wave coffee or an early beer, vintage windows, the sound of the river.

steps.title: A fjord close at Sørenga
steps.description: A courage lap at the swimming pier, or just feet dangling; dinner in Bjørvika — as the Barcode lights fall onto the water.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: City, fjord and forest — the Oslo trio

steps.title: Classic Oslo
steps.description: The one-day flow above: opera, Munch, promenade, Vigeland, Grünerløkka.

steps.title: Fjord day
steps.description: The Bygdøy museums in the morning (Fram and Kon-Tiki — polar and ocean adventures); ferry to Hovedøya for a swim and picnic in the afternoon; a fjord sauna + wharf dinner in the evening.

steps.title: Marka and altitude
steps.description: Metro line 1 to Frognerseteren: a forest walk, a cake break with a view, the Holmenkollen tower on the way down; sunset at Ekebergparken in the evening — farewell with the real landscape of the Scream.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Norwegian is polite and soft; everyone speaks English, but these five melt the ice instantly.

items.meaning: Hello — 'hei hei' is warmer; 'ha det' is goodbye
Thank you — 'tusen takk' means a thousand thanks
Here you go / you're welcome — the waiter sets your plate down with it
Cheers! — the eye contact is Viking heritage, don't skip it
'Warm, pleasant, snug' — Norway's hygge; every candlelit moment is koselig
